readerTitle: Why six players go home and twelve stay all afternoon
caseNote: 일상 장면 (공원 즉석 축구) + 가상 사례 (코워킹 조찬 모임, 병원 근무 교대 앱) + 실제 연구 (Rohlfs 1974, 통신 서비스 수요). 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 임계 질량은 숫자를 서서히 늘려 가는 경사가 아니라 넘거나 못 넘는 문턱이다. 그래서 넓게 퍼뜨리기보다 한곳에 모아 먼저 넘겨야 한다.
misconception: 사용자가 많을수록 네트워크는 저절로 살아난다. 일단 많이 모으면 된다.

sources.text: Rohlfs, J. (1974). A Theory of Interdependent Demand for a Communications Service. Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science, 5(1), 16–37.
'임계 질량(critical mass)'의 물리학적 정의: 연쇄 반응이 스스로 유지되는 데 필요한 최소 핵분열 물질의 양
공원, 코워킹, 병원 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Rohlfs(1974) 논문의 서지 정보(학술지명, 권호, 쪽수)와, 논문이 '충분한 사용자가 모이기 전에는 서비스 가치가 낮다'는 임계 질량 논지를 다룬다는 점을 게시 전에 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 일반적인 서술로만 적었습니다.
3번 카드 차트 수치(7→6→4→3→2, 15→16→19→22→26)는 하향·상향 순환을 보여주기 위한 가상 수치입니다. 카드에 'might move'로 표기했습니다.
즉석 축구 '12명'은 한 팀 6명씩 경기가 성립하는 정도를 가정한 설명용 수치입니다.

cards.title: Why six players go home and twelve stay all afternoon
body: Every Saturday, a few people bring a ball to the park hoping for a pickup game. Some weeks six show up. They kick around, wait, and drift home early.
Other weeks twelve show up. There's a real game. It runs for hours, and players text friends to join.
The gap between those weeks isn't six people. It's whether the game happens at all.

image.label: Two park scenes: a few idle players versus a full game
image.brief: 좌우 분할 일러스트. 왼쪽: 공원 잔디에 6명이 공을 들고 서성이고 몇 명은 가방을 메고 떠나는 중. 오른쪽: 같은 공원에서 12명이 활발하게 경기 중이고 한 명은 휴대폰으로 친구를 부르는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 유니폼 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your founders' breakfast is shrinking.
body: You run a coworking space. You launch a weekly founders' breakfast so members can swap advice and contacts. Week one, 9 of your 300 members come. Week two, 6.
You have time and budget for one push. What do you do?

options.text: Email all 300 members every week and promote it across the city
options.feedback: You'll get more sign-ups, but scattered people come once and rarely return. Each breakfast can still feel half empty.

options.text: Personally recruit 15 regulars who commit to the next six weeks
options.feedback: A small, reliable table makes every visit worth it, so people return and bring others. You trade reach for a breakfast that actually works.

options.text: Add a free hot buffet to draw a bigger crowd
options.feedback: Food fills seats, but people come for the eggs, not each other. When the buffet ends, so may the crowd, and your costs have risen.

cards.title: Same breakfast, two starting points.
body: Here's how attendance might move. Below a certain size, each visit disappoints, so fewer return. Above it, each visit pays off, and people bring others.
Nothing else changed. Only where it started.

cards.title: Critical mass
body: **Critical mass** is the point where a network is useful enough that people stay and bring others without you pushing.
The name comes from physics: the amount of material a chain reaction needs to keep itself going. Below it, the reaction dies out. Above it, it feeds itself.
For a pickup game, that might be twelve players. For your breakfast, maybe fifteen founders who show up every week.

image.label: A tipping line: below it arrows fall, above it arrows rise
image.brief: 가로 점선 하나에 "Critical mass" 라벨. 점선 아래에는 아래로 향하는 화살표와 흩어지는 사람 아이콘, 점선 위에는 위로 향하는 화살표와 서로 손을 잡고 늘어나는 사람 아이콘. 단순한 플랫 인포그래픽.

cards.title: One loop, two directions.
body: In a network, each person's experience depends on who else is there. That experience decides whether they come back.
Below critical mass, the loop runs downward: a thin crowd, a poor experience, fewer return, an even thinner crowd. Above it, the **same loop runs upward**.

Economist Jeffrey Rohlfs described this in 1974 for phone services. A phone is of little use until enough of the people you want to call have one, and early buyers may give up before that point arrives.

cards.title: The right people, not the total.
body: Critical mass is counted from each customer's point of view. A founder doesn't care that 300 members *could* come. She cares whether the people worth meeting are at the table.
That's why 15 committed regulars beat 300 maybes. **Concentrated effort** can cross the line in one place. Spread-out effort can stay below it everywhere.
The line also sits in a different place for each business. A trade marketplace may need enough suppliers that most buyers find what they need on the first search.

image.label: One full table versus many tables with one person each
image.brief: 위에서 내려다본 코워킹 라운지. 왼쪽: 테이블 하나에 15명이 모여 대화 중. 오른쪽: 테이블 10개에 1~2명씩 흩어져 앉아 휴대폰만 보는 모습. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Critical mass can be faked, and lost.
body: Paying people to show up, with free food, discounts or sign-up bonuses, can make a network look full. When the payments stop, you learn whether people came for each other or for the perk.
The loop also runs backward. If key regulars drift away, a network above the line can slide back below it.
And this only matters when customers value each other's presence. A bakery with one customer still bakes good bread.

cards.title: Now it's a shift-swap app for hospitals.
body: Your app lets nurses post shifts they can't work so colleagues can pick them up. A swap only happens if someone on the same ward sees the post in time.
You have 400 nurses ready to try it. How do you roll it out?

options.text: Spread them across 40 hospitals to build presence everywhere
options.feedback: You look national, but each nurse sees only a few colleagues on the app. Posted shifts go unclaimed, and users quit before any ward crosses the line.

options.text: Put all 400 into a handful of wards at two hospitals
options.feedback: Posts get picked up fast, so nurses keep using it and tell other wards. You give up early reach to get proof that it works.

options.text: Launch at 10 hospitals with a cash bonus for every swap
options.feedback: Bonuses will create swaps, but you can't tell real demand from paid activity. Usage may fall the day the bonus ends.

cards.title: Below critical mass, growth leaks. Above it, growth feeds itself.
body: Before chasing more customers, ask where the smallest group is that could cross the line first.
**Try it today:** if your business depends on customers meeting, trading with or helping each other, name the smallest group where that already works. Count how many in it came back last week.
